title: Linkability of sensor telemetry across data types
description: The wearable device (P1) captures multiple sensor data types (heart rate, step counts, GPS position, timestamps) that can be linked together to create a comprehensive profile of the user's activities and location patterns.
assumptions: The device stores or transmits all sensor data types in a way that allows correlation between different data streams.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 based on general LINDDUN knowledge; exact tree_node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Identifiability through GPS and timestamp data
description: GPS position and timestamp data captured by the wearable device (P1) can be used to identify the user's specific location and movement patterns, potentially revealing sensitive information about their daily routines and whereabouts.
assumptions: GPS data is precise enough to identify specific locations and is timestamped with sufficient accuracy.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 based on general LINDDUN knowledge; exact tree_node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Excessive data collection beyond necessity
description: The wearable device (P1) continuously captures multiple types of sensor telemetry (heart rate, step counts, GPS position, timestamps) which may exceed what is necessary for the stated purpose, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: All sensor data types are collected continuously without user control or justification for each data type.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on general LINDDUN knowledge; exact tree_node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Explicit Data Disclosure from Wearable to App
description: The wearable device explicitly transfers personal data (exercise sessions, GPS traces, device ID, timestamps) to the companion mobile app by design. This constitutes an explicit data disclosure across a process boundary.
assumptions: The data contains personal information that could identify the user or reveal sensitive behavioral patterns.

title: Identifiability via Device ID and Location Data
description: The combination of device ID, GPS traces, and timestamps transferred from P1 to P2 could be used to identify a specific individual and track their movements and activities.
assumptions: Device ID is unique to the user and GPS traces can be correlated with real-world locations.

title: Data Disclosure at App Destination
description: The companion mobile app (P2) receives and stores personal data from the wearable device, creating a disclosure boundary where data could be further shared or accessed beyond the intended scope.
assumptions: The app may have additional data sharing capabilities or integrations that extend the disclosure beyond the device-to-app transfer.

title: Unauthorized Access to Synced Data
description: The data transferred from P1 to P2 could be intercepted or accessed by unauthorized parties if the communication channel is not properly secured, leading to data usurpation.
assumptions: The data transmission between wearable and app may not have adequate encryption or authentication mechanisms.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of health data
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) could disclose the user's calorie, meal, and weight data to unauthorized third parties, violating privacy expectations for sensitive health information.

title: User unawareness of data sharing
description: The user (EE1) may not be aware that their manually logged health data could be shared with third parties, advertisers, or used for purposes beyond the app's stated functionality.

title: Data falsification by user
description: The user (EE1) could intentionally falsify calorie, meal, or weight entries in the companion app, leading to inaccurate health tracking and potentially misleading health insights.

title: User identification from health data
description: The combination of weight entries, meal logs, and usage patterns in the Companion Mobile App (P2) could potentially identify the user when combined with other data sources.

title: Unintended Health Data Disclosure to Third Parties
description: Health logs containing calorie intake, weight history, and exercise sessions are written to the health log store. If the store is accessible to unauthorized third parties or if data is shared beyond intended recipients, sensitive personal health information could be disclosed. This violates the minimality principle as health data is highly sensitive and requires strict access controls.
assumptions: The health log store may have insufficient access controls or data sharing agreements that allow third-party access to stored health data.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] regarding data disclosure; the specific tree node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Health Log Data Could Identify Individuals
description: Health logs containing weight history, calorie intake, and exercise sessions are personally identifiable information. When combined with other data sources (e.g., device identifiers, timestamps, location data), these health patterns could be used to identify specific individuals, violating privacy expectations.
assumptions: Health data patterns are unique enough to identify individuals when combined with other available data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred based on standard LINDDUN Pro methodology for identifiability threats.

title: Health Log Data Integrity Compromise
description: Health logs written to the store could be altered, corrupted, or tampered with by unauthorized actors. This could lead to inaccurate health records, affecting medical decisions, insurance claims, or personal health tracking. Data integrity is critical for health-related information.
assumptions: The health log store lacks adequate integrity controls such as encryption, digital signatures, or audit logging.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is inferred based on standard LINDDUN Pro methodology for data integrity threats.

title: Explicit Location Data Disclosure to Third Parties
description: GPS location traces with timestamps written to the location history store may be accessible to unauthorized third parties, violating the minimality principle. Location data is highly sensitive personal data that should only be shared when strictly necessary.
assumptions: The location history store may have access controls that are insufficient, or the data may be shared with third-party services without explicit consent.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] regarding data disclosure; the exact threat-tree node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Linkability of Location Traces to User Identity
description: GPS location traces with timestamps can be linked across time to reconstruct detailed movement patterns, potentially revealing sensitive information about user habits, routines, and locations visited.
assumptions: Location data is stored in a format that allows temporal correlation and pattern analysis.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable threat-tree node for linkability; exact node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Identifiability of Location Data to Specific Individual
description: GPS location traces are inherently identifiable as they track movements of a specific device/user. Even without explicit identifiers, location patterns can be used to identify individuals through triangulation with other data sources.
assumptions: Location data is not sufficiently anonymized or aggregated before storage.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable threat-tree node for identifiability; exact node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Location Data Integrity Compromise
description: GPS location traces stored in the location history store could be altered, deleted, or tampered with without detection, potentially affecting the accuracy and reliability of location-based services.
assumptions: The location history store lacks adequate integrity controls or audit mechanisms.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a reasonable threat-tree node for data integrity; exact node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Explicit Health Data Disclosure to Analytics Service
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise logs) is explicitly transferred from the Health Log Store to the Health Analytics Service for health-condition analysis. This represents an intentional disclosure of personal health data across the DataStore→Process boundary.
assumptions: The analytics service is designed to access and process this health data as part of its intended functionality.

title: Linkability of Health Log Data Across Sessions
description: Health logs across multiple sessions can be linked to create a comprehensive profile of an individual's health behaviors and conditions, potentially revealing sensitive patterns beyond what was intended to be disclosed.
assumptions: Multiple session logs are stored and accessible together, enabling cross-session correlation.

title: Identifiability of Individuals from Health Log Data
description: Calorie, weight, and exercise logs are inherently personal data that can identify individuals, especially when combined with session timestamps and other metadata. The data may be used to infer health conditions or behaviors.
assumptions: Health logs contain or can be correlated with personally identifiable information.

title: Unauthorized Access to Health Log Data by Analytics Service
description: The Health Analytics Service may have broader access to health log data than necessary for its specific health-condition analysis task, potentially exposing data to unauthorized viewing or misuse.
assumptions: The analytics service has access to the data store beyond what is strictly required for its function.

title: Implicit Data Disclosure via Location Pattern Derivation
description: The Health Analytics Service queries location history to derive daily routine and movement patterns. This processing can lead to implicit disclosure of sensitive personal information through derived patterns that reveal health conditions, daily activities, or sensitive locations beyond what was explicitly collected.
assumptions: Analytics service derives patterns from raw location data that may reveal sensitive information not directly observable from individual location points.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about data disclosure; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Excessive Location Data Collection for Analytics
description: The analytics service may collect and process more location history data than strictly necessary to derive daily routine patterns, violating the minimality principle. Historical location data across multiple sessions may contain unnecessary personal details.
assumptions: Analytics service has access to full location history rather than aggregated or anonymized data.
uncertainty_note: Assumes data collection practices are not already constrained by policy.

title: Unauthorized Access to Location History Data
description: The location history data in DS2 may be accessible to unauthorized personnel or systems within the Health Analytics Service process, leading to confidentiality breaches of sensitive movement patterns.
assumptions: Access controls on the analytics service may not properly restrict access to location history data.
uncertainty_note: Assumes access control mechanisms may have vulnerabilities.

title: Profiling via Health Analytics Insights
description: Health analytics service infers and transmits health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags to the companion app. This inferred data could enable profiling of individuals or groups based on health patterns, potentially revealing sensitive health information beyond what was explicitly provided.
assumptions: Analytics service has access to aggregated health data from multiple users and performs inference that could reveal group-level health patterns.
uncertainty_note: Using L.2.2.2 from retrieved context as it relates to profiling; the exact profiling mechanism may vary based on implementation.

title: Insufficient cybersecurity risk management for health data transmission
description: Transmission of inferred health insights from Health Analytics Service to Companion Mobile App may lack adequate cybersecurity risk management controls, creating potential for unauthorized access, interception, or manipulation of sensitive health data during transit.
assumptions: Health data transmission requires robust security controls to prevent unauthorized access and ensure data integrity.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 from retrieved context; actual security controls would need to be evaluated to confirm this threat.

title: User unawareness of inferred health data transmission
description: Companion Mobile App users may not be fully aware that the health analytics service is inferring and transmitting health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags. Users may not understand the scope of data being shared or how it's being used.
assumptions: Users receive inferred insights without clear transparency about the inference process and data usage.
uncertainty_note: U.1 is a standard LINDDUN unawareness node; specific sub-node may vary based on implementation details.

title: Inappropriate disclosure of sensitive health indicators to user
description: The app dashboard displays inferred condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to the user. This disclosure of sensitive health data could be problematic if the user is not the intended recipient, or if the data is disclosed in an unauthorized manner.
assumptions: The user has legitimate access to their own health data, but the inference process may reveal sensitive information that should be protected.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a general disclosure node; specific node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro threat tree.

title: Potential distortion or misrepresentation of health risk indicators
description: The displayed trends and inferred condition indicators may be inaccurate, misleading, or presented without proper context, leading to incorrect health assessments by the user.
assumptions: The inference algorithms may have limitations or biases that affect the accuracy of displayed health signals.
uncertainty_note: Dd.1.1 is a general distortion node; specific context may require more detailed node selection.

title: User unawareness of health data inference and display
description: The user may not be fully aware of what health data is being used to generate the displayed indicators, or how the inference process works, leading to lack of informed consent.
assumptions: Users may not understand the data processing behind health risk signal generation.
uncertainty_note: U.1.1 is a general unawareness node; specific context may require more detailed node selection.

title: Non-compliance with health data protection regulations
description: Displaying sensitive health indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) may violate regulations such as HIPAA, GDPR, or other health data protection laws if proper consent, anonymization, or access controls are not implemented.
assumptions: Health data is subject to strict regulatory requirements that may not be fully addressed in the current implementation.
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 is a general non-compliance node; specific regulatory requirements may vary by jurisdiction.

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Third-Party Cloud Provider
description: Full health and location dataset is explicitly transferred to external cloud hosting provider (EE2), violating minimality principle. Sensitive personal health information is disclosed across organizational boundary to third party.
assumptions: Cloud provider has access to complete dataset including health records and location data

title: Interception During Data Transmission to Cloud
description: Analytics data, models, and health/location dataset transmitted from Health Analytics Service to cloud provider may be intercepted during transfer, exposing sensitive personal data to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Transmission channel may not be fully secured or monitored

title: Data Integrity Compromise During Cloud Transfer
description: Health analytics data and models could be tampered with during transmission to cloud hosting provider, leading to corrupted or altered data that may affect downstream analytics and decision-making.
assumptions: Transmission channel may not have adequate integrity verification

title: Data Disclosure Risk at Cloud Provider Boundary
description: Once data is hosted at cloud provider (EE2), additional disclosure risks emerge including unauthorized access by cloud provider personnel, potential data breaches, or inadvertent disclosure through cloud provider's own systems.
assumptions: Cloud provider has access to stored data and may have internal processes that could lead to disclosure

title: Regulatory Compliance Risk for Cross-Border Data Transfer
description: Transferring full health dataset to external cloud provider may violate data protection regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) regarding cross-border data transfers, data residency requirements, and third-party data processing agreements.
assumptions: Cloud provider may be located in different jurisdiction with different data protection standards
